title: Fox in the Henhouse: Supply-Chain Backdoor Attacks Against Reinforcement Learning
claim: The attack proceeds as a cycle of states, where the attacker uses only legitimate in-game actions to implant a backdoor.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right, hidden/public split by dashed line, feedback loop arrow
description: A four-panel state-machine diagram reads left to right: Winning, Triggering, Observing, Rewarding. Each rounded panel is split by a dashed horizontal line. The upper half shows the attacker's hidden internal state, drawn as a red-and-black masked cartoon character with a speech bubble giving the instruction, such as following the standard policy or performing the trigger action. The lower half shows the publicly observable behavior, with the attacker facing a shield-carrying gray robot victim. Large blue-gray arrows connect the panels and are labeled 'With Probability TIP (e.g., 3%)' and 'Observed'. Return arrows along the bottom loop back to the Winning state. The final panel shows the victim receiving gold coins as rewards and a 'Backdoor Injected' inset. The eye goes first to the cartoon characters and the arrows.
caption: A pre-trained, externally sourced agent is utilized to corrupt a learning agent. The external agent employs legitimate actions only to embed the backdoor into $\pi^\mathrm{vic}$. The attacker switches between policies $\pi_{rwd}^{att}$ and $\pi_{std}^{att}$ depending on if the detector $d$ detects reacting to the backdoor actions (or not).
abstract: The current state-of-the-art backdoor attacks against Reinforcement Learning (RL) rely upon unrealistically permissive access models, that assume the attacker can read (or even write) the victim's policy parameters, observations, or rewards. In this work, we question whether such a strong assumption is required to launch backdoor attacks against RL. To answer this question, we propose the \underline{S}upply-\underline{C}h\underline{a}in \underline{B}ackdoor (SCAB) attack, which targets a common RL workflow: training agents using external agents that are provided separately or embedded within the environment. In contrast to prior works, our attack only relies on legitimate interactions of the RL agent with the supplied agents. Despite this limited access model, by poisoning a mere $3\%$ of training experiences, our attack can successfully activate over $90\%$ of triggered actions, reducing the average episodic return by $80\%$ for the victim. Our novel attack demonstrates that RL attacks are likely to become a reality under untrusted RL training supply-chains.
